transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-28 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood), Sofia Alvarez (Cobalt Head of ML), Marcus Lee (Cobalt Platform), Priya Nair (Cobalt Procurement)
-- Auto summary (first-pass): Discussed pilot commercial guardrails (how many credits, what the pilot covers), scope of benchmark workloads and success criteria, timeline to procurement, and what metrics the SE team needs to run early throughput/latency runs. Action items captured and calendar for contracting intro.

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — appreciate the tight schedule this week. Quick roll call?
[00:09] Sofia: Hey, Sofia here. Marcus is on, Priya's on. Thanks Jordan.
[00:13] Marcus: Marcus, hey.
[00:15] Priya: Priya joining.
[00:18] Maya: Maya from Redwood. Liam's also on to help with reliability questions.
[00:22] Jordan: Cool. Goal for today: nail down pilot commercial guardrails we talked about in the email thread — credits, what the pilot covers (test vs production-like), and the runway to contracting. Also capture workloads for benchmarking.

[00:38] Sofia: High level, we have three use cases — 1) in-store search re-rank, 2) checkout assistant for fraud flags, and 3) product copy generation. We want to validate latency and cost on real-ish traffic and measure QA against our internal evals.
[00:55] Marcus: For infra constraints, we're currently 80% on GKE with private clusters; we need either VPC peering or a private endpoint for the private deployment tests. We're evaluating Redwood hosted first, then Dedicated if it looks good.
[01:12] Jordan: Got it. On credits: our typical pilot package for accounts this size is 120k token credits plus 100k embedding units, but that's flexible depending on benchmarking needs. That usually covers 2-4 weeks of heavy benchmarking and a light production smoke test.
[01:33] Priya: Can you explain what you mean by token credits? Our procurement team thinks in dollar budgets.
[01:40] Jordan: Sure — shorthand is credits tied to token/embedding consumption. We'll attach a dollar-equivalent in the pilot terms doc; for contracting we'll map credits to a not-to-exceed dollar cap for the pilot.
[01:50] Sofia: Are credits refundable if the pilot fails? We need guardrails.
[01:54] Jordan: Not refundable per se, but we can classify the pilot as evaluation; if it doesn't meet success criteria we won't auto-roll into paid Reserved capacity. We can propose a credit carryover clause if both sides agree on scope extension. I'll put that in the draft terms.
[02:10] Maya: From the SE side, we need the canonical workloads and a seed prompt set. The more representative the data, the more accurate the cost/latency estimates. For the re-rank flow we need top-10 candidate sizes, average tokens per query, and average session QPS.
[02:28] Marcus: We'll export a week of telemetry. Expect heavy tail — p95 seq length ~420 tokens, median ~85.
[02:35] Maya: Great, that helps. For benchmark targets we usually run two profiles: a latency-first profile (p95 < 200ms on hosted for 1k qps) and a cost-driven profile (minimize cost per 1k tokens with batching). We'll share the benchmark template.
[02:54] Speaker 1: (inaudible) this is also where KV cache matters for checkout assistant — if cache hits we save a lot.
[03:01] Jordan: Good point. We can scope a KV caching experiment as part of the pilot; that would affect cost outcomes.
[03:08] Sofia: On success criteria, we have three buckets: functional accuracy metrics (for re-rank MAP@10 improvement of +6% over baseline), latency SLOs (p95 < 220ms for critical flows), and economics (cost per 1M tokens < $X, TBD after you give the dollar mapping).
[03:28] Jordan: That's a sensible split. We'll make the pilot terms explicit: success criteria met => Redwood and Cobalt agree on a path to Reserved capacity or a 6-month committed discount. If not met, option to extend pilot for extra credits with mutually agreed scope.
[03:44] Priya: From procurement, what's the expected contracting path? We need a short pilot amendment to an MSA or a one-off pilot agreement? Also, any standard SOC/ISO attestation docs?
[03:55] Liam: We typically do a one-page pilot addendum plus our machine terms. For enterprise customers we include SOC 2 Type II and ISO summaries; full reports go through an NDA process. For private deployments, we also do a security review.
[04:12] Priya: We will need SOC2 and encryption at rest details. Also KMS integration specifics — do you support customer-managed keys?
[04:20] Maya: Yes, for Redwood Private we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption and a managed KMS but can discuss bring-your-own-key for Dedicated/Private. We'll include KMS integration notes in the security pack.
[04:33] Jordan: I'll attach a link to the security dossier in the follow-up.
[04:36] Marcus: On timeline: we want to start benchmarks next week and have a go/no-go in three weeks.
[04:42] Jordan: Timeline check — pilot kickoff (benchmarking) by 2025-11-03, results and go/no-go review by 2025-11-21, contracting intro as soon as results look promising — procurement sync the week of 2025-11-03?
[04:55] Priya: The week of 11/3 works for a contracting intro meeting. We'll need an estimated SOW and pilot coverage beforehand.
[05:03] Jordan: We'll send the pilot terms and a simple SOW draft. On credits, if the initial 120k token credit looks insufficient after you share workloads, we can increase credits or extend the pilot duration. We just need the run profile to align credit sizing.
[05:18] Sofia: Another variable — we may want to test a quantized model variant for cost reasons. Does that change the credit mapping?
[05:25] Maya: Slightly, yes. Quantized variants reduce token compute cost but may change latency. We'll treat model variants as separate benchmark buckets and map credits to each run so accounting is clear.
[05:36] Jordan: About fallbacks: if dedicated capacity isn't ready we promise routing to compatible hosted variants with SLOs spelled out in the terms. We'll put a fallback policy in the pilot addendum.
[05:48] Marcus: For private endpoint tests: how long does setup typically take? We need an estimate for our infra calendar.
[05:55] Liam: Private endpoint for VPC peering takes ~2-3 weeks for onboarding and firewall changes; Dedicated on-prem can be 6+ weeks depending on network approvals. For the pilot we recommend hosted first and then a short Dedicated spike if results justify it.
[06:11] Speaker 1: (background) maybe test a smaller sample in the hosted path to validate before we attempt peering.
[06:16] Jordan: Exactly, a smoke test on hosted then scale-up runs.
[06:19] Maya: We will also run a small throughput test to validate p95 latency at a scaled load — we'll need a ramp plan and a prepared runbook to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[06:29] Sofia: On reporting, we expect per-route dashboards and token-level breakouts. Do you provide that in the pilot?
[06:35] Jordan: Yes — Console access for the pilot includes token-level cost breakdowns, per-model latency histograms, and traces for failures. We'll provide a 2-week retention in the pilot and can extend if needed.
[06:46] Priya: Anything we should be aware of on terms — auto-renewal traps? We want explicit opt-in to move to paid commitments.
[06:53] Jordan: No auto-renew into committed capacity. The pilot addendum will require explicit signing of a Reserved capacity quote to convert. I'll make that clear.
[07:01] Marcus: For benchmarks, what's the turnaround for Redwood running the first full suite once we hand over telemetry?
[07:07] Maya: If telemetry and prompts arrive within 48 hours, we can run an initial benchmark within 3 business days for hosted runs; Dedicated spikes take longer. We'll document run parameters and results in a shared spreadsheet.
[07:18] Jordan: I'll also include a cost sensitivity table: how credits map to dollar spend under three modeled profiles (baseline, batched, quantized).
[07:27] Sofia: Good. Also, who signs the pilot — is it AE signature or procurement?
[07:30] Jordan: For pilot-level credits we can do a one-page acceptance signed by Procurement (Priya). The MSA is the larger ask for production.
[07:36] Priya: Ok, we prefer a minimal pilot addendum that captures data use, credits, and termination. We'll review your draft.
[07:43] Jordan: Perfect. Recap and explicit next steps: Jordan will send pilot terms, security dossier link, and cost mapping by 11/03. Maya will send benchmark harness and example prompts by 10/31. Cobalt (Marcus/Sofia) to share telemetry and seed prompts by 10/30. Procurement intro meeting scheduled for week of 11/03.
[07:59] Sofia: Sounds good. One more question — are there limits on parallel experiment runs under the pilot? We might want multiple teams testing concurrently.
[08:06] Maya: The credit accounting supports multiple parallel experiments; we just ask that you coordinate ramp windows so we don't hit concurrency headroom unexpectedly. We'll include a recommended experiment schedule in the runbook.
[08:18] Jordan: Alright, I'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs. Thanks all.
[08:22] Marcus: Thanks everyone.
[08:24] Priya: Thank you.
[08:25] Meeting ends.
